meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock'?
meta.ogDescription: A 1958 Rolls-Royce advertisement from Ogilvy’s agency. Three reference works, three different wordings.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1911–1999 · British advertising executive, founder of Ogilvy & Mather
answer.sourceLine: This is the headline of a Rolls-Royce press advertisement from 1958, produced by David Ogilvy’s New York agency. Wikipedia’s article on Confessions of an Advertising Man ↗ records that Ogilvy called it his “best headline ever.” We could not examine the advertisement, and our sources do not agree on its exact wording — so this is attributed rather than verified.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: David Ogilvy’s New York agency, Ogilvy, Benson & Mather
Wording varies between references; original not examined

source.excerpt: At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock.
trail: Wikipedia ↗ states that Ogilvy’s firm “promoted the Rolls-Royce automobile with the famous headline, ‘At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock’” — our display wording, word for word.

Wikiquote ↗ carries the line sourced to “Rolls-Royce print ad, 1958” and calls it “sometimes referred to as the most famous headline in advertising history” — but prints it without “new,” and offers no page or archive locator.
Wikipedia’s article on Confessions of an Advertising Man ↗ reports Ogilvy calling it his “best headline ever,” citing page 123 of the book, and prints a third transcription of the line.

Wikipedia’s article on the agency ↗ states that the firm reopened as Ogilvy, Benson & Mather in 1954, which is the name it carried in 1958, and that it became Ogilvy & Mather in 1964 on merging with the London agency Mather & Crowther.
All three agree on the advertiser, the year and the substance. They disagree on the words, which is why this page stops short of verified: we could not reach a scan of the advertisement to settle it.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording Wikipedia’s article on Ogilvy ↗ prints, and it is the form that circulates. Wikiquote ↗ gives it without the word “new,” and Wikipedia’s article on the book ↗ gives it in title case as “At Sixty Miles an Hour, the Loudest Noise in the New Rolls-Royce Comes from the electric clock.” We did not see the advertisement itself and do not assert which is the printed line.

author.name: David Ogilvy
author.heading: About David Ogilvy
author.metaLine: 1911–1999 · British advertising executive, founder of Ogilvy & Mather
author.bio: David Mackenzie Ogilvy founded his advertising agency in New York in 1948 with $6,000 and financial backing from his brother Francis, then managing director of the London agency Mather & Crowther. By 1963 Ogilvy, Benson & Mather billed $55m across 19 clients, Rolls-Royce among them. Time called him “the most sought-after wizard in today’s advertising industry” in 1962, and he is widely called the father of advertising.

misattribution.heading: Often misquoted
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is credited with this line. The problem is narrower and stranger: the three reference works we could reach print it three different ways, and none of them shows the advertisement.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ drops the word “new” and cites only “Rolls-Royce print ad, 1958” — no publication, no page, no scan.

items.who: “At Sixty Miles an Hour… the New Rolls-Royce”
items.why: The article on Confessions of an Advertising Man ↗ renders the headline in title case with “Sixty” spelled out and “the New Rolls-Royce” for “this new Rolls-Royce.”

misattribution.truthLine: The advertisement is real, it ran in 1958, and it came from Ogilvy’s agency. What we could not do is read the advertisement, so we do not assert which of the three printed wordings appeared on the page.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Ogilvy founded his agency in New York in 1948 with $6,000 and backing from his brother Francis. By 1963 it was billing $55m across 19 clients — Chase, Standard Oil of New Jersey, Shell, KLM, Guinness and Rolls-Royce among them — and Time had already called him “the most sought-after wizard in today’s advertising industry.”

The Rolls-Royce headline is the advertisement people cite when they argue that a specific, checkable fact sells better than an adjective. It names a speed, a noise and a clock, and lets the reader do the arithmetic about everything it does not mention.
detailsBody: The advertisement was followed by 719 words of body copy, later increased to about 1,400 after readers responded well to the first — a detail Wikipedia’s article on the book ↗ takes from Confessions of an Advertising Man itself.

What we could NOT establish, and therefore do not assert anywhere on this page: whether Ogilvy composed the sentence or took it from somewhere else. The claim is widely repeated online; the sources that would settle it were not reachable from here, and we would rather leave a gap than fill it from a search result.
context.pull: Ogilvy called it the best headline he ever wrote.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikipedia states that Ogilvy’s firm promoted Rolls-Royce with the headline "At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock", and gives Ogilvy’s dates as 23 June 1911 – 21 July 1999.
Wikiquote sources the line to a 1958 Rolls-Royce print advertisement but prints it without the word "new".

Wikipedia’s article on Confessions of an Advertising Man reports Ogilvy calling this his "best headline ever" (citing p. 123), prints a title-case variant of the wording, notes the 719-word body copy later raised to 1,400, and records the agency founded in 1948 with $6,000 and billing $55m across 19 clients including Rolls-Royce by 1963.
Wikipedia states the agency reopened as Ogilvy, Benson & Mather in 1954 and became Ogilvy & Mather in 1964, supporting the agency name given for the 1958 advertisement.
